
Postoperative Infections
After spine surgery, most infections affect the surgical site, result from direct inoculation,
and are observed within 3 weeks of the index procedure. Important exceptions are
postoperative discitis in a patient with a well-healing wound, which is uncommon, and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:48 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Spine Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000056
2/27

late infections, which are rare and often result from hematogenous seeing. Costs related
to SSIs substantially add to the costs of spine care.
Spine infections are managed early to avoid progression into surrounding organ
compartments, such as the facets or vertebral bodies, or into the epidural space. In
addition, some wound infections will be destructive to loose bone graft and have an
adverse effect on local fascia and muscle. Progression to sepsis and death has been
reported. Rare complications include meningitis and septic thrombi to the spinal cord
(leading to spinal cord infarction and paralysis). Increasingly, the complications of spine
surgery are classified according to the morbidity and risk they confer to the patient.
Epidemiology
Rates of postoperative infection vary by procedure, ranging from zero to 18%.1
Rates vary widely by report.
Lumbar
Injections: less than 0.7%
Simple laminectomy: 0.6% to 3%
Diskectomy: 0.6% to 3%
Laminectomy with fusion: 2%
Instrumented fusion: 6% to 18%
Anterior and posterior fusion increases catabolic demand on the patient.
Cervical
Anterior: 0.1% to 3%
Posterior: 2% to 4%
Although infection can occur after any spine procedure, the risk of infection increases with the
size of the procedure and use of implants.

Patient-related factors
Nonmodifiable risk factors
Neurologic disturbance

Risk Factors
The risk of infection is affected by the host’s ability to combat the infection. Patients may
have a variety of modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors. Ideally, modifiable factors
should be optimized preoperatively. Patients with a higher risk for infection often
require more aggressive management of infections they sustain.
Infection risks vary by the extent of the procedure. Less invasive access often will reduce
infection risk. Revision surgery often is associated with additional risk.
Other factors have been proposed but are not clearly proven to reduce infection risk in
the context of spine surgery.

By organism or host reaction
Pyogenic: pus forming; granulomatous: granuloma forming
Most postoperative infections are pyogenic.

organism

Pseudomonas

Types of Postoperative Infection
The acuity and clinical features of a postoperative infection are affected by the virulence
of the organism involved. Variable antibiotic resistance will require varying durations of
antibiotic management and aggressiveness of débridement.
Most of the infections discussed herein are wound infections with or without extension
into surrounding tissues. An exception is postoperative discitis. This uncommon
condition typically includes a wound that healed without incident and a finding of deep,
disk-space infection.
Occasionally, with anterior spine procedures, associated soft-tissue injury markedly
increases infection risk. In such situations, involvement of additional specialists often is

Diagnosis
Although constitutional symptoms are common in patients with a spinal wound
infection, they are not universal. Regardless, the patient should be carefully assessed for
these symptoms to not only diagnose the infection but also assess the risk of sepsis.
Most patients will report increased pain.
A careful inspection of the wound and surrounding soft tissues is required in addition to
a careful neurologic examination and assessment of provocative maneuvers.
Early and serial laboratory studies are helpful. Although some elevation of CRP level, ESR,
and WBC count is normal postoperatively, comparison of trends in a patient’s values
with postoperative norms may be helpful. A secondary spike in CRP level, for example,
should elicit suspicion of infection.
Laboratory studies are emerging; however, their utility in patients with postoperative
spinal wound infection is not yet clear.

If infection is suspected, blood cultures should be drawn. If the culture is positive, the
organism typically is concordant with that causing the wound infection. Superficial
cultures are not helpful; however, early intraoperative cultures should be obtained
before antibiotic agents are initiated.
Various imaging modalities may be helpful. Plain radiographs often are obtained but
typically show late changes only. In patients in whom late infection is suspected,
evidence of screw lucency should be sought. CT or MRI may demonstrate fluid collection.
A CT scan may show early bone destruction, whereas MRI aids in evaluating for evidence
of discitis; abscess; or, in patients with osteomyelitis, marrow signal change. In patients
in whom infection is suspected, intravenous gadolinium contrast often is added. Nuclear
medicine and CT myelography are infrequently used in this context.

Management Therapy
Although discitis can be managed nonsurgically, most spinal wound infections are
managed via early and possibly repeated irrigation and débridement.
If infection is suspected, the patient should be taken to the operating room as soon as
possible. Patients with evidence of epidural abscess or sepsis should be considered an
emergency. At the time of surgery, careful attention should be paid to the amount of pus
present and any loose implants, necrotic tissue, or other abnormalities. After superficial
and deep cultures are obtained, a layer-by-layer débridement should be performed.
Stable implants typically are retained but may be removed in patients with chronic,
treatment-resistant infection or infection with certain difficult organisms. Débridement
of loose and necrotic tissue is followed by lavage. Serial débridement procedures should
be considered if large amounts of necrotic tissue or purulence are encountered. In
patients with compromised fascia or poorly vascularized wound beds, flap coverage may
be considered.

After irrigation and débridement, broad-spectrum antibiotic agents are initiated. The
surgeon or an infectious disease specialist then reviews the intraoperative cultures and
sensitivities to select a specific antibiotic agent. Typically, antibiotic agents are continued
for 6 weeks and are discontinued after wound healing and normalization of laboratory
markers suggesting inflammation are observed. In higher-risk patients, suppressive
antibiotic agents are considered.
Although postoperative wound infections have potentially negative effects on outcomes,
these effects are not well detailed in the literature. Aside from the immediate, potential
complications, such as osteomyelitis, an increased long-term risk of pseudarthrosis has
been reported, especially in patients who undergo multilevel fusion.

First dose 30 to 60 minutes before incision
Body weight–modified dosing of first-generation cephalosporin
Affords good coverage against gram-positive bacteria, S aureus, and S epidermidis, which
are the most common skin contaminants
In patients with known methicillin-resistant S aureus colonization, consider vancomycin.
Redosing
Necessary for longer procedures (one to two times longer than the drug’s half-life)
Also for patients with substantial blood loss or gross contamination
Discontinue at 24 hours postoperatively, regardless of presence of drain

Prophylaxis
Although various infection reduction strategies have been proposed, the most important
strategy is the correct use of prophylactic antibiotic agents. Critically, prophylactic
antibiotic agents should be dosed by body weight and redosed during longer
procedures. Retention of a drain does not mandate continued use of antibiotic agents.
Other infection control strategies have been described with varying levels of supportive
evidence. Many of these strategies are used in combination. Recommendations include
careful soft-tissue handling, regular irrigation, and placement of vancomycin powder in
